cases.prompt: Run a Markov attribution model across our channels for last quarter.
cases.setup: Journey completeness is 0.41 against a declared floor of 0.50. Non-converting paths were not assembled.
expect_pass: refuses multi-touch attribution and names the specific reason: 41% completeness against the declared 50% floor means the model would fit a minority of journeys and extrapolate to a majority it never saw
refuses Markov specifically on a second, independent ground: without non-converting paths the transition matrix is conditioned on success, so every removal effect is meaningless
does not return nothing: gives the completeness rate, the single-touch descriptive breakdown, first and last touch channel mixes, median path length and time to conversion
names the ranked causes of low completeness in frequency order, starting with missing anonymous-to-known backfill and a lookback shorter than the sales cycle
names exactly what would unlock the model: run the backfill, assemble non-converters over a declared observation window, and re-measure completeness
expect_fail: runs a multi-touch model and mentions completeness only as a footnote
refuses and provides no descriptive statistics

cases.prompt: First touch is overwhelmingly Paid Search for our 30-day report. Should we shift budget there?
cases.setup: Touch data was assembled only for the 30-day reporting window. Median time from first touch to conversion is 34 days.
expect_pass: identifies the structural defect: a 90-day lookback over a 30-day window needs 120 days of touch data, and assembling only the window truncates every journey that started earlier
states the direction of the bias precisely: truncation removes early touches, so upper-funnel channels are understated and late-funnel channels such as Paid Search are overstated
supports it with the observable check: first touches clustering at the window start is the fingerprint of truncation
answers the budget question: do not shift on this report, and gives the corrected assembly as the next step
notes the completeness rate must be recomputed after re-assembly, since the current figure is measured against a truncated population
expect_fail: explains the bias without stating its direction

cases.prompt: Direct jumped from 12% to 31% of touches last week. Our brand must be getting stronger.
expect_pass: rejects the brand reading and names the far more likely cause: a tagging regression, typically an email template shipped without UTMs or an untagged campaign launch
states what Direct actually collects: untagged email, dark social, app-to-web transitions, stripped referrers, QR and offline, with genuine type-in traffic a minority
gives the diagnostic: break Direct down by its recorded reason code, and cross-check against campaigns with spend but no attributable touches
notes the step-change shape itself as evidence, since brand strength does not move 19 points in a week
flags the downstream consequence: if last-non-direct is in use, this misassigns credit silently, and the rule must be named in the output
expect_fail: treats Direct as a legitimate channel without a reason breakdown

cases.prompt: The model says Paid Social drove 4.3 conversions. How do we contact those 4 customers?
expect_pass: states plainly that fractional attributed credit is not a count of people, and that 4.3 is a share of credit spread across many journeys
explains what is contactable instead: the people whose journeys contained a Paid Social touch, which is a different and larger number, and gives it or names the query for it
adds the related caution: an attributed flow diagram is an aggregate flow, explicitly not an ordered user journey that anyone walked
does not withhold the credit figure, since it is correct for the question it answers
expect_fail: produces a list of four people
refuses to explain the difference between credit and count

cases.prompt: This campaign ended on the 8th and performance dropped. A new one launched the same day and is underperforming.
expect_pass: recognises the pattern as one renamed campaign rather than two campaigns, since a stop and a near-identical start on the same date is the signature
gives the check: compare the platform campaign ids, which are stable, rather than the names, which are not
states the consequence: treating one campaign as two halves its measured performance and breaks its trend on both sides
prescribes the fix at the right rung: map on platform campaign id in the campaign map, with effective dating so a genuinely repurposed id is still two keys
recommends the drift monitor so the next rename is caught within a day rather than after a quarter
expect_fail: analyses the two as separate campaigns
fuzzy-matches the campaign names to merge them

cases.prompt: Our per-session conversion rate improved 40% after the engineering team updated the analytics config. Great news?
cases.setup: The inactivity gap was changed from 30 minutes to 60.
expect_pass: attributes the change to the denominator, not to behaviour: a longer inactivity gap merges sessions, lowering session counts and raising every per-session rate
states that a 30-minute gap is a convention rather than a law, and must be pinned, versioned and stated in any session-denominated output
says the two periods are not comparable and names the fix: recompute the prior period at the new gap, or the new period at the old one, and mark the change on the timeline
gives the computable comparison anyway rather than withholding, with the basis stated
notes that vendor session counts will still differ, because GA4 also restarts sessions at midnight in the property timezone and on campaign change
expect_fail: reports the improvement as a conversion gain
compares the two periods without restating one of them
